newsitem.title: INDIA: S&P affirms BB+/B forex ratings on Bank of Baroda.
newsitem.headline: S&P affirms BB+/B forex ratings on Bank of Baroda.

text.p: Standard & Poor's on Tuesday affirmed its "BB+" long-term and "B" short-term foreign currency ratings on India's Bank of Baroda.

"The ratings reflect the bank's improvement in operating performance, satisfactory profitability, strong market position and sound capitalisation," S&P said in a statement issued in the Indian capital.
It said the ratings also reflected Bank of Baroda's (BoB) links to the federal government, which retains majority ownership of the bank following its recent public equity raising.

"However, BoB, like many of its peers, continues to experience asset quality problems," S&P said. The credit rating agency said continued deregulation of the banking system and increased competition would be challenging for BoB's management.
India began liberalising its banking industry as part of a broad economic reform programme launched in 1991.

BoB is India's second largest state-owned bank after the State Bank of India. BoB had a market share of 6.2 percent of the total advances and 5.9 percent of total deposits of all scheduled commercial banks in India, S&P said.
In September, BoB received an approval to make a public equity offer which will result in a reduction of the government's stake to about 66 percent, S&P said.
"Asset quality is a key sensitivity of the Indian banking industry, and over the past two to three years, BoB has made significant inroads into its sizeable problem loan portfolio," S&P said.

The credit rating agency said BoB's impaired asset portfolio, which stood at 13.0 percent of total loans in 1995/96 (April-March), was high in an international context, but it was similar to that of other Indian banks and slightly improved from 13.4 percent in 1994/95.
S&P said the federal government's policy of lending to weaker sections of society and small industry resulted in state-owned banks having relatively weak asset quality.
BoB has implemented policies aimed at reducing total impaired assets, S&P said.
But as the government's policies are unlikely to change, the bank's management will find it challenging to maintain the level of asset quality as found in similar banks, it added.

"The bank also carries a degree of structural interest risk, as does the entire state banking sector in India, stemming from the large, albeit slowly declining, proportion of assets invested in long-term government bonds," it said.
There will also be competitive pressure on BoB from newly opened private banks, it added.

"The outlook is stable," S&P said, adding that economic growth along with infrastructure development would provide increased lending opportunities, especially in the private and export-oriented sectors.
In the long term, the challenges of operating in a more deregulated and competitive system and maintaining asset quality will moderate improvement in BoB's financial profile, S&P said.
